sumber: KSSM Form 5 English DSKP (CEFR-aligned). All passages and questions are written for the app; medium to hard.

nota.t: Tenses show time and aspect. Present simple for habits and facts; present continuous for actions now; present perfect for past actions linked to now (have/has + past participle); past simple and past continuous for finished and ongoing past actions; past perfect for an earlier past; and future forms (will, be going to, present continuous for arrangements).
By the time we arrived, the film had started. (past perfect for the earlier action)

Conditionals: zero (facts: If you heat ice, it melts), first (real future: If it rains, I will stay home), second (unreal present: If I had wings, I would fly) and third (unreal past: If I had studied, I would have passed). Relative clauses use who, which, that, whose and where; non-defining clauses add extra information between commas.

The passive voice focuses on the action or receiver: be + past participle (The bridge was built in 1990). Reported speech shifts tenses back and changes pronouns and time words: 'I am tired,' she said → She said that she was tired.
Active: The students cleaned the hall. Passive: The hall was cleaned by the students.

Modals express ability (can, could), permission (may), obligation (must, have to), advice (should, ought to) and possibility (might). Gerunds (-ing) follow verbs such as enjoy, avoid and finish; infinitives (to + verb) follow want, decide and hope. Some verbs change meaning: stop smoking vs stop to smoke.

t: Tenses, conditionals, relative clauses, passive, reported speech, modals, gerunds and infinitives.

nota.t: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle to make a new meaning: give up (stop), look after (care for), run out of (have no more). Idioms are fixed expressions whose meaning is not literal: a piece of cake (easy), break the ice (start a conversation).

Collocations are words that naturally go together: make a decision, do homework, heavy rain, strong coffee. Word formation builds new words with prefixes (un-, dis-, mis-) and suffixes (-ness, -ment, -able, -ful): happy → unhappy → happiness.

v.c: Word formation with prefixes and suffixes

t: Phrasal verbs, idioms, collocations, word formation.

nota.t: For reading comprehension, skim for the main idea, scan for specific details, infer meaning from context, understand the writer's purpose and tone, and work out the meaning of new words from clues in the sentence.

t: Skim the text for the main idea
Check your answer against the text

nota.t: Formal writing (letters of complaint, reports, articles for a school magazine) uses polite, complete sentences and no contractions or slang. Informal writing (emails to friends, blogs) is friendly and personal. Every text needs an opening, clear paragraphs and a suitable closing.

v.c: Formal and informal openings and closings

nota.t: Linkers connect ideas: addition (moreover, furthermore), contrast (however, although), cause and effect (therefore, as a result), sequence (firstly, finally) and examples (for instance). A good paragraph has a topic sentence, supporting details with examples and a concluding sentence.

t: Formal and informal register; linkers; paragraphs; emails, letters, articles, reports.

nota.t: For poetry, look at the theme, the speaker, tone, imagery and literary devices (simile, metaphor, personification, repetition). For prose (short stories and novels), study the plot, setting, characters, conflict, point of view, themes and moral values, and support every point with evidence from the text.

t: Use PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link
Quote briefly and explain how it shows the point
Poetry and prose terms: theme, persona, tone, imagery, plot, conflict.
